newsitem.title: USA: Dollar reverses recent slide, climbs on German comments.
newsitem.headline: Dollar reverses recent slide, climbs on German comments.

text.p: The dollar rose sharply Tuesday as a string of pro-dollar statements from German central bank officials took the market by surprise after a series of significant losses.

The dollar started to climb after Bundesbank council member Edgar Meister said the current dollar/mark rate below 1.50 marks was not appropriate, echoing earlier comments from fellow council member Hans-Juergen Krupp that a firmer dollar might seem more appropriate.
But market makers remained sceptical that the dollar's resurgence would last until Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer welcomed the dollar's rebound.
"People waited for Tietmeyer to speak to see if he would add any credibility to the earlier Bundesbank comments," said Bob Houck, vice president at Norwest Bank in Minneapolis.
"Once he collaborated, short (sellers) started covering their positions and the bulls jumped on board."

The dollar shot up to an intraday high of 1.5090 marks after Tietmeyer spoke. It fetched 1.5080 marks in late trading, up from 1.4937 late Monday. The dollar also gained to 1.2690 Swiss francs from 1.2545 Swiss francs late Monday.

"It's pretty clear that at least some members of the Bundesbank, if not all, are uncomfortable with a weak dollar and conversely a strong mark," said Michael Faust, global portfolio manager at Bailard, Biehl and Kaiser in San Francisco.
"A strong mark complicates an already delicate economic and political situation for Germany," he added.
Bundesbank members Meister and Tietmeyer urged credible adherence to the strict entry criteria for European Monetary Union, stoking worries about the prospect of the proposed union.
However, the concern failed to spark major buying of marks, which dealers turn to as a safe haven amid any signs that the EMU would unravel, they said.

"It appears Germany will take a tact, even if they are tough on the EMU criteria, of trying to keep the dollar stable," said Mark Gargano, managing director of currency derivatives at First Union National Bank in Charlotte, N.C.
The Bundesbank comments overshadowed remarks last week from key Japanese officials that raised concerns Japan might be changing its longstanding strong-dollar, weak-yen policy.
The dollar rose to 111.50 Japanese yen in late trading from 111.10 late Monday, falling for four consecutive sessions.

Many dealers doubt that the yen will soon strengthen against the dollar, as Japanese officials expect, due to the large difference between U.S. and Japanese interest rates, which makes the dollar more attractive to investors.
"Japan doesn't want dollar/yen going higher, but they also want to keep their rates down so I don't think anyone buys it," Gargano said.
Dealers also cited market talk that U.S. President Bill Clinton could make significant headway toward a balanced U.S. budget over the next few months as helping the dollar.
The dollar also fell to Canadian $1.3330 from C$1.3344 late Monday.
